meta.blurb: A tired man falls asleep in 1897 and wakes in 2100 to learn that he owns half the world. Everyone cheers his name, but a clever friend has plans of his own. Can the Sleeper save the people who trust him?
meta.bible: Graham: a young Englishman of 1897, worn out by worry and sleeplessness; falls into a trance and sleeps 203 years; brave, curious and honest. Isbister: a cheerful young artist who meets Graham on the cliffs at Boscastle and finds him in the trance. Warming: Graham's practical cousin, who takes charge of his sleeping body and his money. Howard: the man who is with Graham when he wakes and tells him the year; serves the Council. Ostrog: the Boss, a strong white-haired leader of the working people, who seems a friend but plans to rule the world himself. Helen Wotton: a brave young woman who tells Graham the truth about the poor and about Ostrog and helps him escape. White Council: the group that grew from the trustees and rules half the world in the Sleeper's name. Labour Company: the huge organisation whose poor workers wear blue. Black Police: the soldiers Ostrog brings in to crush the people. Boscastle: the seaside village in Cornwall where Graham falls asleep. Cornwall: the county in the far south-west of England. England. London: in 2100 a huge city under one great roof, with moving roadways and giant signs. Facts: the year of the trance is 1897 and the year of waking is 2100, so Graham sleeps 203 years; the city's power comes from huge wind vanes on the hills; flying machines are common; Graham's fortune, left in trust, has grown until he owns half the world. Ending: the people win, Ostrog's plan fails, and Graham falls from the sky; the book leaves it unclear whether he lived. Voice and tone: a retelling of the 1910 novel by H. G. Wells in clear, vivid prose; wonder at first, then growing unease; violence is mentioned plainly with no gore.

A1A2: In 1897, a young man named Graham could not sleep at night.
On the cliff, he met a kind artist called Isbister.
He tried many things, but still he could not sleep.
One night Graham finally slept, but he did not wake up.
Doctors came, but nobody could wake the sleeping man.
Isbister wrote to Graham's cousin Warming, who came quickly.
Warming put Graham in a safe room and watched over him.
Years went by, and Graham slept on while the world changed.
Graham's money grew and grew, year after year.
The men who kept his money became the rulers of half the world.
In the year 2100, Graham opened his eyes at last.
A man in strange clothes told him to stay calm.
Howard said, “You have slept for two hundred and three years.”
Everyone Graham knew had been dead for a very long time.
Howard told him, “You are the master of half the world.”
The Council wanted to keep him in his room.
Graham looked around the room and saw many strange things.
Far away, Graham heard a strange sound like a great crowd.
Graham tried to leave, but a guard stopped him at the door.
When a door was left open, he ran out into the hall.
He stepped out and saw a huge city under one roof.
Below, many people in blue rode on moving streets.
The people saw him and shouted, “The Sleeper has woken!”
Guards tried to catch him, but the crowd saved him.
The crowd took him to a big hall and cheered him.
A strong man called Ostrog came and shook his hand.
Ostrog said the Council was bad and the people were poor.
The people were now fighting the Council's men in the streets.
Graham saw the fighting and felt afraid for the people.
By morning, the Council had lost, and Graham was free.
Ostrog said, “Rest, and let me do the work.”
Graham saw huge wind machines on the hills, giving power to the city.
Graham learned that many poor people worked for the Labour Company.
A brave young woman named Helen spoke to him about the poor.
Graham went to see how the poor people lived.
Graham made a promise to help the poor people.
Graham rode in a flying machine and rose into the sky.
From the sky, he saw big cities and empty land.
Ostrog brought in soldiers called the Black Police to keep order.
Graham saw that Ostrog gave all the orders now.
Helen warned Graham that Ostrog was a danger to the people.
Graham asked Ostrog what he planned, and Ostrog smiled.
At that moment Graham decided to speak to the people himself.
Helen helped Graham to escape from Ostrog's guards.
Graham stood before the workers and spoke to them.
The people took up weapons and got ready to fight.
News came that Ostrog's soldiers were flying toward the city.
Graham jumped into a flying machine and flew up.
The machines fought in the sky above the great city.
Graham hit the enemy machine, and the people won the day.
B1B2: Graham is a young Englishman who has worked too hard and worried too much. For many nights he has hardly slept, so he has come to the seaside village of Boscastle to rest.
One morning on the cliff Graham meets Isbister, a friendly young artist who is staying in the village. Graham tells him that he has not slept for many nights, and Isbister listens with growing worry.
Graham has tried long walks, warm drinks and a dark room, but none of these things has worked. Each night he lies awake and listens to the waves, and he begins to feel afraid.
At last, late one night, Graham falls into a sleep so deep that nothing can disturb it. In the morning Isbister finds him lying stiff and pale, and he cannot wake him however loudly he calls.
Several doctors hurry to the inn, and they examine Graham with great care. His heart is still beating, but very slowly, and nothing they try can wake him.
Isbister finds the address of Graham's cousin, a man named Warming, and writes to him at once. Warming arrives, looks at the sleeper sadly, and takes charge of everything.
Warming has Graham carried to a safe room, where he lies in a glass case, warm and quiet. He also puts Graham's money in the care of trusted men, who are called trustees.
Years pass, and then whole decades go by, while the world outside changes in many ways. Isbister and Warming grow old and die, but Graham lies in his case, still sleeping and hardly changed.
The trustees invest Graham's money wisely, and it grows a little more every year. After two hundred years it has become so large that it is hard to imagine.
In time the trustees form a group called the White Council, and the Council gains power over cities and countries. It rules half the world in the name of the Sleeper, who knows nothing about it.
One quiet day in the year 2100, Graham's eyes open slowly after two centuries of sleep. He is lying in a strange white room, and a soft light shines from the ceiling.
A man bends over the bed and speaks to him in a strange, quick way. His name is Howard, and he tells Graham to lie still and not to be afraid.
Graham asks in a weak voice where he is and what year it is. Howard answers gently that it is the year 2100, and that Graham has slept for two hundred and three years.
Graham thinks of Isbister, of Warming, and of everyone he ever knew. They are all long dead, and he feels more alone than any man has ever been.
Howard explains that the money left behind by Graham has grown beyond all measure. Graham is now the owner of half the world, though the Council rules in his name.
Howard says that the Council wishes Graham to rest and to see no one yet. The doors of his rooms are watched, and Graham begins to wonder whether he is a master or a prisoner.
Graham is given food and warm new clothes, and he wanders about his rooms in wonder. Everything is different, from the soft light to the machines that do things he cannot understand.
Late in the day Graham hears a deep roaring noise far away, like a great crowd. Howard hurries out of the room, and his face is full of worry.
Graham tries to leave and see the city, but the guards at the door will not let him pass. He understands at last that he is a prisoner, however grand the title they have given him.
Later that day a door is left open by mistake, and Graham does not wait. He slips through it and runs along a bright corridor with his heart beating hard.
Graham comes out onto a high balcony and looks down into an enormous hall. Below him lies a whole city, covered by a single great roof.
The streets below are moving like rivers, and they carry thousands of people dressed in blue. Huge signs shine high above, shouting out their advertisements in bright letters at everyone who passes.
A man in the crowd looks up and sees him, and then he points and cries out. Within moments thousands of faces are turned upwards, and the cry spreads that the Sleeper has woken.
The Council's guards run after Graham and try to drag him back. However, the crowd rushes forward, pushes the guards aside, and carries him away on its shoulders.
The crowd carries Graham through the streets to a great hall where thousands wait. They cheer him, bow to him, and call him their master, and he does not know what to say.
A strong man with white hair pushes through the crowd and greets Graham warmly. He is Ostrog, a great leader of the working people, and he says that he has long been waiting for the Sleeper.
Ostrog explains that the Council has ruled badly and has kept the people poor and afraid. He offers to help Graham take the power into his own hands.
News comes that the people have risen against the Council and are shouting Graham's name. Fighting has begun in many parts of the city, and Graham feels the weight of what he has started.
Through the night the battle goes on, and Graham sees people fall in the streets. He is horrified, because nothing in his quiet life before the trance has prepared him for it.
By morning the Council's men have been beaten, and the White Council has fallen. Ostrog announces to the cheering people that the Sleeper is now the master of the whole world.
Ostrog tells Graham to rest and to learn about the new world, while he looks after the daily work of ruling. Graham is glad to agree, for he knows almost nothing about the age he has woken into.
Graham learns that the city's power comes from huge wind vanes standing on the hills. They are enormous machines that turn in the wind and send energy to every home and factory.
Graham asks who all the people in blue are, because he has seen so many of them. He is told that they are the poor, who work for the huge Labour Company all their lives and own almost nothing.
A young woman named Helen Wotton asks to speak with Graham in private. She is brave and honest, and she tells him how hard life is for the people in blue.
Graham asks Helen to show him the lives of the poor with his own eyes. They walk through narrow, noisy streets where whole families live in tiny rooms.
Graham feels deeply ashamed, because his own money has helped to make these lives so hard. He promises Helen that he will use his power to make things better.
Graham asks to try one of the new flying machines. It rises smoothly above the roofs, and Graham shouts with joy as the city falls away beneath him.
From the sky Graham sees that the villages he once knew have almost disappeared. In their place are giant cities, with wide stretches of empty land between them.
Graham hears that Ostrog has called in a strong force of soldiers, known as the Black Police. They have come from far away, and they obey no one except Ostrog.
Graham begins to notice that everyone obeys Ostrog and that nobody really listens to him. When he asks for something, the answer is always that it must wait for a better time.
Helen finds Graham alone and warns him that Ostrog is not his friend. The Boss means to rule the world himself, using Graham's name, and he will crush the people if they resist him.
Graham goes to Ostrog and asks him plainly what he means to do. Ostrog answers smoothly, but he does not deny that he holds all the real power.
Graham knows that the people are his only real friends in this strange new world. He decides to speak to them himself, before Ostrog can find a way to stop him.
With Helen's help, Graham slips away from Ostrog's guards in the middle of the night. They hurry through dark passages and out into the streets, where the people are waiting.
In a great hall full of workers, Graham stands up and tells them the truth. He says that he will not be a puppet, and that he will fight beside them for their freedom.
The workers arm themselves and gather in the streets, ready to face Ostrog's soldiers. Graham moves among them and sees that they are afraid, but that they will not turn back.
Messengers arrive with terrible news that the Black Police are flying toward the city in great machines. If those soldiers are allowed to land, the people will have no chance against them.
Graham has learned a little about flying, and he does not hesitate. He climbs into a machine, grips the controls, and rises into the sky to meet the enemy.
The people's flying machines meet the enemy over the city, and a great battle begins. Machines fall burning from the sky, and Graham flies through the smoke towards the largest enemy machine.
Graham drives his machine into the largest enemy machine and brings it down. The people have won, but Graham falls from the sky, and the book never says whether he lives.
C1C2: In 1897, a young Englishman named Graham arrived in the little Cornish village of Boscastle, wrung out by weeks of worry and sleepless nights. The sea air and the quiet were supposed to cure him, but his mind went round and round like a mill wheel and would not stop. He wandered the cliffs with hollow eyes, longing for nothing in the world so much as a single night of ordinary sleep.

On the cliff path Graham fell into talk with Isbister, a cheerful young artist who was painting the coast and who took pity on the haggard stranger. Graham confessed that sleep had abandoned him entirely, that no medicine had helped, and that he felt his mind slowly coming apart. Isbister, who had never seen a man so worn, advised him to rest and to be patient with himself.

Graham tried every remedy he could think of: long walks until his legs ached, warm drinks, darkened rooms and drops that a chemist had sold him. None of them did anything but leave him more exhausted, and each dawn found him staring at the ceiling with a dull, burning ache behind his eyes. The sea outside murmured on and on through the dark, as though it were mocking him from a great and peaceful distance.

Sleep came at last, but it was not the gentle sleep that Graham had longed for, for it closed over him like deep water and held him fast. When Isbister came to the room the next morning he found his new friend lying as stiff and pale as a statue, with no answer for his shouting or for his shaking. A cold fear crept over the young artist as he realised that this was no ordinary rest.

The doctors who hurried to the inn were puzzled and a little frightened, for the man in the bed was neither dead nor truly alive. His heart beat so faintly that they had to press their ears to his chest to hear it, and his body was as cold as marble. They gave the condition a name, a trance, but none of them could say when, or whether, he would ever wake.

Among Graham's papers Isbister found the name of a cousin, a careful and practical man called Warming, and he wrote to him without delay. Warming came by the next train, stood for a long while looking down at the motionless figure, and then began quietly to make arrangements. Whatever happened to his cousin, it seemed, would now be settled by a man with a pen and a great deal of patience.

Warming had the sleeper carried to a safe and quiet room, where he was laid in a case of glass to keep out the dust and the cold. He placed Graham's fortune in the hands of trustees, men whose task was to guard it and to make it grow while its owner slept. Nobody imagined, least of all Warming, that the arrangement might one day change the whole world.

The years rolled by, and then the decades, and the world outside the glass changed beyond all recognition. Isbister and Warming grew old and were laid in their graves, and the very language people spoke began to alter, yet the sleeper lay on without a single wrinkle. He had become a curiosity first, then a legend, and at last a kind of sacred secret kept by men who had never known him.

The trustees were shrewd men, and they bought land and houses, factories and shipping lines, so that Graham's fortune swelled like a river after rain. Each generation of them passed the work to the next, and each found the sleeper's wealth greater than the last had left it. By the end of two centuries it had grown beyond anything that Warming could ever have dreamed.

Over the generations the trustees grew into the White Council, a small and powerful group that owned the great companies, the ships and the very streets of the cities. It governed half the world, and it did so openly in the name of the Sleeper, whose face few had ever seen. The whole machine of the age was driven by money that belonged to one man who did not know it existed.

Then, on a day in the year 2100, the sleeper's eyelids trembled and slowly opened, and the first thing Graham saw was a smooth white ceiling that he did not know. He lay still, afraid to move, while a strange light poured down from above without any lamp that he could see. Nothing in the room was familiar to him, and for a long moment he thought he must still be dreaming.

A man in unfamiliar clothes was standing at the bedside, and he spoke in an accent so altered that Graham could barely follow him. He gave his name as Howard and urged the sleeper, again and again, to stay quiet and to be calm. His eyes were kind, but they were also watchful, and Graham felt that he was being studied.

When Graham found his voice, he asked where he was and how long he had lain there, and Howard answered with great care. It was the year 2100, he said, and the sleeper had slept through two hundred and three years without moving. Graham stared at him, the words falling into his mind like stones into a deep well, and he could find nothing to say.

His thoughts flew back to the cliffs of Cornwall, to Isbister and to Warming and to every face he had ever known, and he understood that they were all dust. The loneliness that settled on him was greater than any he could have imagined, for he had lost not a country or a home but an entire age. Yet he was alive, and with that strange knowledge a small, stubborn curiosity began to stir in him.

Howard then told him a thing that made his head spin, that the fortune left in trust had grown beyond all counting and that Graham was now the owner of half the world. The White Council, he explained, ruled in the Sleeper's name, and the whole great world looked to him as the source of its power. Graham laughed aloud at the absurdity of it, and then he stopped laughing, because Howard did not smile.

The Council, Howard admitted, would prefer that Graham stayed quietly in his rooms for the present and spoke to no one except the few men it had chosen. Graham, who was beginning to recover his courage, noticed that the doors were guarded and that no one had said when he might leave. He suspected, with a chill, that a master who cannot walk out of his own door is not much of a master.

They brought him food that he did not recognise and clothes of a soft cut and colour that no tailor of his own age would have imagined, and he found that he could eat and dress without help. He walked about the suite with his hands behind him, peering at the lights, the walls and the strange devices that answered to a touch. The world, he began to see, had not merely grown older, it had grown into something wholly new.

As the hours passed, a low and distant roar began to reach his ears, like the sea breaking on a faraway shore, but it was louder and more restless. Howard heard it too, and his composure vanished, for he hurried from the room with a word of apology and the door shut hard behind him. Graham stood listening, and the sound seemed to him to be calling his name.

Graham went to the door and demanded to be taken out into the city, but the guards only bowed and begged him to wait for the Council's pleasure. He argued with them, then ordered them, then pleaded with them, and not a single one of them moved from his place. It was a bitter lesson, and he learned it quickly: the owner of half the world was kept in a gilded cage.

At last a servant's carelessness left a door ajar, and Graham, who had been waiting for just such a chance, slipped through it before anyone could raise a hand. He ran along a bright and curving passage, his new clothes flapping around him and his heart pounding like a drum. Behind him he heard shouts, but ahead of him was the unknown, and he preferred it to the cage.

Graham burst out onto a high gallery and stopped, for he was looking down upon a space so vast that he could hardly take it in. Below him, under a single immense roof, lay a whole city of towers and bridges, shining with light. It was the London he had once known, he realised, swallowed and made over beyond recognition.

The streets themselves were in motion, great belts of roadway sliding past one another at different speeds, and they carried thousands upon thousands of people dressed in the same blue cloth. Overhead, enormous signs blazed and flickered, pressing advertisements upon every passer-by in letters taller than houses. Graham, who had known the quiet lanes of Cornwall, felt that he had stepped into the mouth of a roaring machine.

One man in the crowd looked up and saw the strange figure on the gallery, and a word began to pass from mouth to mouth like a spark running through dry grass. Within a minute the roadways were full of faces turned upward, and the roar that Graham had heard before became a mighty shout that rang around the whole hall. The Sleeper had woken, and the people had been told for generations that this day would come.

The guards reached the gallery and tried to seize him, but they had no chance against the tide that was now rising from below. Hands reached up to him from every side, and in a moment Graham was lifted from his feet and borne along over the heads of the crowd like a swimmer on a wave. He was frightened, and yet he was also stirred, because every face around him was glowing with hope.

The crowd bore him through street after street to a great hall, where thousands more were waiting, and they greeted him with a sound like thunder. They called him master and protector, and some wept openly, and some held up their children for him to see. Graham, who an hour before had been a prisoner, found himself a king without knowing how it had happened.

A broad, strong man with white hair forced his way through the press and bowed to Graham with a calm and powerful smile. He introduced himself as Ostrog, the Boss, a leader of the working people, and he said that he and all his followers had long prayed for this day. Graham liked the man at once, and he did not stop to ask himself whether such a smile might hide something else.

In a quiet room, Ostrog explained that the Council had grown proud and cruel, that it had grown rich on the labour of millions, and that the people longed for a master who would set them free. All Graham had to do, he said, was to take the power that was already his by right, and the people would follow him. It sounded so reasonable and so noble that Graham agreed, and the word of the Boss seemed like firm ground.

Before long, messengers burst in with news that the whole city had risen, that the people were marching on the Council's strongholds and that Graham's name was on every tongue. From a high window he watched the lights move and the crowds swirl, and he heard the muffled crack of fighting in the distance. He had wanted only to escape a locked room, and now the fate of a nation seemed to rest on his decision.

Through the long night the fighting raged across the city, and Graham stood among Ostrog's men and saw the flashes and heard the cries and watched the wounded carried past. He was no soldier, and nothing in his quiet life before the sleep had prepared him for the sight of so many people suffering because of his name. Still, he told himself that a cruel power was being broken, and that the price might be worth paying.

When dawn came, the Council's defenders had been beaten or had fled, and the White Council that had ruled in Graham's name for so long was suddenly nothing at all. Ostrog stood before the cheering people and declared that the Sleeper was now the master of the world, and that all the Council's power was in his hands. Graham looked out over the happy faces, and for a short time he allowed himself to believe that the story was over.

Ostrog urged Graham not to tire himself with the dull business of government, and proposed that he should rest and learn about the new world while the Boss himself took care of the daily work of ruling. Graham, who knew nothing of the age he had woken into, accepted gratefully and thanked him for his kindness. It did not occur to him that a man who holds the reins of an empire does not easily let them go.

From a high roof he was shown the great wind vanes, towering white machines that stood in ranks upon the hills and turned slowly in the breeze. Their turning gave the city its light, its heat and the strength to drive its moving streets, and not a single coal fire was needed to keep it alive. Graham thought of the smoke of old London and felt, for the first time, a sense of honest admiration.

When Graham asked about the multitudes in blue, he was told that they were the workers of the Labour Company, a vast organisation that housed, fed and clothed the poor in return for their whole lives. They were born into its keeping, they laboured at its machines, and they died owing it more than they had earned. It sounded to Graham less like a company than like a kind of slavery with a polite name.

One day a young woman named Helen Wotton came to Graham and spoke to him with a boldness that surprised him. She told him that the people who cheered his name were poor, hungry and bound in debt, and that they had risen in the hope that he would free them. Her eyes were steady, her words were plain, and Graham could not look away from either.

Graham, who would not be satisfied with reports, asked Helen to show him the poor with his own eyes, and she led him down into the crowded lower streets. There he saw whole families packed into tiny rooms, children with pale faces, and workers who stared at him with weary wonder. He had been lord of the world for days, and he had never known any of this.

The sight filled him with shame, for it was his own fortune, grown and multiplied, that stood behind the Company and the chains it laid on the poor. He vowed to Helen that he would not rest until he had done what he could to set those people free. She said nothing, but the light in her face told him that she believed him.

Graham, hungry for every wonder of the new age, begged to be taken up in one of the flying machines, and soon he was rising through the roof of the world with the wind in his face. The machine climbed smoothly and steadily, and the great city dropped away beneath him like a map spread out on a table. He laughed out loud, like a boy let out of school, and for a moment his troubles were forgotten.

From high above, Graham saw an England that he could barely recognise, with its little villages gone and its fields turned to open grassland or to the grey spread of vast cities. The country he had loved had been folded up and put away, and the people had been gathered into a few enormous hives. He felt a sudden ache for the quiet green lane and the cliff path above the sea.

Back in the city Graham heard that Ostrog had summoned a disciplined force of soldiers, known as the Black Police, from distant parts of the world to keep order. They were strangers to the city and its people, and they answered to Ostrog alone, which did not seem to Graham a reassuring thing. A first small doubt entered his mind, and it was one that he could not easily put away.

As the days passed, Graham noticed that every order came from Ostrog and that every door was opened or closed at the Boss's word. When he asked to visit the Labour Company's workers, or to speak to the people, he was told gently that the time was not right and that he must wait. He had been named master of the world, and he was beginning to feel like a clever ornament.

Helen slipped to his side when no one was near and told him, in a low and urgent voice, that Ostrog was not the friend he seemed. The Boss intended to rule the world himself and to use the Sleeper as a mask, she said, and if the people resisted him, the Black Police would be turned upon them without mercy. Graham felt that he had known it in some part of himself for days, and that only his pride had kept him from looking.

Graham went to Ostrog and demanded to know exactly what he intended, and the Boss answered with a smile as smooth and cool as a polished stone. He spoke of order and of necessity and of the foolishness of the crowd, but he did not deny that he held the real power, and he made it plain that the Sleeper would be wise to be content. In that moment Graham saw the true face of the man who had called him master.

Graham understood that his only real strength lay with the people who had carried him through the streets, and that he must speak to them before Ostrog could bind him altogether. He had no army and no weapon, but he had a name that thousands loved, and he meant to use it. It was a desperate plan, and he knew that it might cost him his life.

Helen knew the hidden ways of the great building, and she led Graham through narrow passages and down unlit stairs while the guards searched in the wrong places. Twice they had to press themselves against a wall as footsteps went past, and twice Graham thought that his heart would burst. Then, at last, a door opened on the noise and the light of the city, and they were out.

In a great hall packed with workers, Graham climbed onto a platform and told them everything, that Ostrog had betrayed them and that he, the Sleeper, would never be a puppet in anyone's hand. His voice shook at first, but as he went on the words came with a force that he had never known in himself. When he had finished, the hall rose as one person, and the roar of it shook the walls.

All through the night the workers armed themselves with whatever they could find and gathered in the streets, and Graham walked among them, hearing their quick breaths and their whispered jokes. Many of them were afraid, and not one of them had ever fought in a war, but they were fighting now for something that had never been theirs before. Graham knew that this was both the best and the most terrible hour of his strange new life.

At dawn the messengers rushed in with terrible news that a fleet of flying machines was racing toward the city, carrying the Black Police. If the soldiers were allowed to land, the people's hastily gathered army would be swept away in an hour, and the Boss would be master of the world. There was only one hope left to them now, and it lay high above their heads, in the open sky.

Graham had learned only a little of flying, but there was no one else to do what had to be done, and he did not hesitate. He climbed into a machine, took the controls in his hands, and drove it upward into the morning, with Helen's face and the shouting of the people still ringing in his mind. Below him the city shrank to a bright toy, and ahead of him the enemy fleet appeared like a line of dark birds.

The two fleets met high above the city, and the sky became a storm of engines, smoke and flying fragments, while the people watching from the streets held their breath. Machines on both sides fell burning out of the air, and Graham steered through the chaos with a recklessness that frightened even himself. Straight ahead of him he saw the largest of the enemy machines, and he knew what he had to do.

Graham drove his machine straight into the great enemy flyer, and the shock of the blow tore the sky apart, scattering the fleet and breaking Ostrog's last hope of ruling the world. Below, the people raised a cry of victory that rolled from one end of the city to the other, for the Black Police would never land. Graham himself fell, and there the story leaves him, tumbling through the light, while the reader is left to wonder whether he lived.
